a: Many have already set their hand
p: Luke knows earlier written accounts. Most scholars think Mark was one of them.
b: Luke opens by admitting he is not the first. The "many" who tried to set the story in order are not named. On the majority view of the Synoptic Problem, one of them was Mark, which Luke follows closely in much of 3:1–24:12; another may be the sayings source scholars call Q, or Matthew itself on the Farrer view. Luke does not say the earlier accounts were wrong. The verb (epecheirēsan, "set their hand to") is neutral in Greek prefaces, though some readers hear a hint that the earlier attempts fell short of what Luke now offers. The church fathers sometimes took it as a swipe at the false gospels of later heretics (Origen, Homilies on Luke 1), but the books Luke means were clearly earlier than his own and used by him.

t: A prologue in the style of Greek historians
p: Verses 1–4 are one long, polished Greek sentence, the most classical in the New Testament.
b: The first four verses are a single balanced sentence of the kind educated Greek writers put at the head of a book: a nod to earlier writers, the author's own qualifications, the addressee, and the purpose. Historians such as Josephus (Against Apion 1.1–3) and writers of technical handbooks on medicine or engineering opened this way, and Loveday Alexander has shown that Luke's preface is closest to those practical handbooks: modest, businesslike and written for a patron. Then, at 1:5, the style changes abruptly to the Bible-like Greek of the Septuagint ("It happened in the days of..."), as if Luke deliberately steps into the world of Israel's Scriptures. The prologue covers Acts too (Acts 1:1).

p: The verb can mean events fully accomplished, or promises brought to fulfillment. Luke may mean both.
b: Peplērophorēmenōn comes from a verb meaning "to bring to full measure." It can mean "fully carried out" (things that have happened) or "fulfilled" (promises that have come true), and Luke's whole story is about God's promises being fulfilled (4:21; 24:44). It can also mean "fully believed" (as in Romans 4:21), which the KJV's "most surely believed among us" follows; most modern scholars think "accomplished" or "fulfilled" fits the context better. "Among us" includes Luke and his readers: the events are not finished but still working themselves out in the church that Acts will describe.

a: saw it with their own eyes from the beginning
p: Luke does not claim to be an eyewitness himself, but to depend on people who were.
b: The Greek autoptai ("self-seers") is the word behind "autopsy." Luke places himself in the second generation: the eyewitnesses "passed on" (paredosan, the word for handing on tradition, as in 1 Corinthians 15:3) what they had seen. "From the beginning" probably means from John's baptism, the starting point Acts 1:21–22 sets for an apostle. Richard Bauckham argues that the Gospels stay close to named eyewitnesses who were still living when they were written; many other scholars think the tradition passed through more hands and was reshaped in preaching. Either way Luke's claim is about his sources, not about himself.

p: The eyewitnesses became "attendants" of the word, as a helper serves a master.
b: Hypēretēs is an assistant or attendant: the synagogue attendant of 4:20, the temple guards of Acts 5:22, John Mark as helper of Barnabas and Paul (Acts 13:5). The risen Jesus chooses Paul "as my helper and my witness" (Acts 26:16), with the same word. "The message" is ho logos, "the word," which this site renders "the message" when it means the Christian preaching (as in Mark 4:33 and in Acts). Some early Christians, such as Origen, read logos here as Christ the Word of John 1:1, whom the apostles saw; most modern readers take it as the preached message.

p: Kathexēs need not mean strict date order. Luke may mean an order that persuades.
b: Kathexēs means "one after another, in sequence." It does not have to mean exact time order: Luke moves stories around compared with Mark (the rejection at Nazareth comes first, 4:16–30; compare Mark 6:1–6), and in Acts 11:4 Peter explains "in order" what happened to him so that his hearers will accept it. Many scholars think Luke means a well-arranged, coherent account, whose order itself helps the reader see what God was doing. Others think he does claim a more careful time order than his predecessors. The word links back to the "account" of 1:1: Luke offers a better-arranged one.

p: A real man of some rank, probably Luke's patron. His name means "friend of God."
b: "Most excellent" (kratiste) is the title Luke later uses for the Roman governors Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25), so Theophilus was probably a man of social standing, perhaps the patron who paid for the book to be copied, as was common for books addressed to someone. The name, "friend of God" or "loved by God," was common among both Jews and Greeks. Origen (Homilies on Luke 1) suggested that every reader who loves God is a "Theophilus," and some modern readers take the name as symbolic, but most scholars think a real person is meant. Guesses that he was a high priest (a Theophilus was high priest AD 37–41, Josephus, Antiquities 18.123) or a Roman official are possible but unprovable. Acts 1:1 drops the title, perhaps meaning nothing.

a: kept careful track of all these things from the start
t: Researched, or followed as they happened?
p: Luke may mean he investigated the events, or that he kept close track of them over a long time.
b: Parēkolouthēkoti literally means "having followed alongside." Most translations take it as research: Luke checked the facts. Henry Cadbury argued that it means Luke had been in touch with the events as they unfolded, that is, he was a participant in part of the story (fitting the "we" passages of Acts). Anōthen can mean "from the beginning," "for a long time," or, in other contexts, "from above," and a few early writers read it as Luke claiming inspiration from above; that sense does not fit a preface about sources. "Careful" renders akribōs, "accurately, carefully." The Plain's "kept careful track of" keeps the sense of following events closely and leaves the method open: research afterward, or watching as they happened.
orig: παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς (parēkolouthēkoti anōthen pasin akribōs)

t: Certainty: the last word of the sentence
p: Asphaleia, "security, firm ground," is the goal of the whole book.
b: The long Greek sentence ends on its key word, asphaleia: safety, firmness, certainty. Luke wants Theophilus to see that what he has been taught rests on solid ground. The same family of words closes Peter's first sermon: "the whole house of Israel must know beyond doubt" (asphalōs, Acts 2:36), and appears where Roman officers want to find out "for certain" what is true about Paul (Acts 21:34; 22:30; 25:26). Luke writes as a historian, but the certainty he means is more than facts checked: it is confidence that God's plan has really been carried out.

t: Taught as a believer, or informed by rumors?
p: The verb is the root of "catechism." It can mean instruction in the faith, or simply reports one has heard.
b: Katēchēthēs gives English "catechize." In Acts 18:25 Apollos "had received instruction in the way of the Lord," and Paul uses it of teaching in the church (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 14:19). But in Acts 21:21, 24 the same verb means rumors that "have been reported" about Paul. If the first sense is meant, Theophilus is a Christian who needs assurance; if the second, he may be an interested outsider, even an official, who has heard things about the Christians and needs an accurate account. Most scholars think he had received Christian instruction.

a: Back when Herod was king of Judea
p: Herod ruled the Jewish lands for Rome from 37 to 4 BC. The story begins before his death.
b: This is Herod the Great, who held the title "king of Judea" from the Roman Senate (40 BC) and ruled from 37 BC until his death, usually dated 4 BC from Josephus' account (Antiquities 17.167, 191). Luke uses "Judea" here for the whole Jewish homeland, including Galilee. Matthew also places Jesus' birth under Herod (Matthew 2:1), one of the few details the two birth stories share, which is why most historians date the birth to about 6–4 BC. The census of 2:2 makes this harder; see the note there. Herod's sons appear later in Luke (3:1; 23:7).

p: The priests served in 24 divisions by turns. Abijah's was the eighth.
b: 1 Chronicles 24:7–19 lists twenty-four families of priests, each to serve in the temple in turn; the eighth lot fell to Abijah (1 Chronicles 24:10). By the first century each division served a week at a time, about twice a year, plus the great feasts. There were thousands of priests (Josephus, Against Apion 2.108, speaks of four tribes of priests of more than five thousand each), most of whom lived in towns outside Jerusalem and came up for their week. Lists of the courses were later carved on synagogue walls, and the Dead Sea Scrolls contain calendars of their service. Attempts, ancient and modern, to date Jesus' birth from Zechariah's week of service rest on too many guesses to be reliable.

a: one of the daughters of Aaron
p: Elizabeth also came from the priestly family. Her name is that of Aaron's own wife.
b: Priests could marry any Israelite woman of good standing (Leviticus 21:7, 14), so marrying a priest's daughter was a mark of honor, and John is a priest's son from both sides. "Elizabeth" is the Greek form of Elisheva, the name of Aaron's wife, "Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab" (Exodus 6:23). Luke opens his Gospel inside Israel's priesthood and temple, and he will end it there (24:53). For the Jewish reader this is a story that begins in the heart of Israel's worship, not against it.

a: They walked in all the Lord's commands and rules
p: Luke describes a faithful Jewish couple keeping the Torah, and praises them for it.
b: "Righteous" and "blameless" are Old Testament words of praise for Noah (Genesis 6:9), Abraham (Genesis 17:1) and Job (Job 1:1). To "walk" in God's commands is a Hebrew way of saying "to live by" them. Luke presents Torah-keeping as goodness, not as a burden to be escaped. Paul uses the same word of himself before he followed Jesus: "as to righteousness under the law, blameless" (Philippians 3:6). Christian readers have sometimes set this verse against Paul's teaching that no one is righteous (Romans 3:10); most interpreters see no conflict: Luke means faithful lives within the covenant, not sinless perfection.

p: Luke tells John's birth in the pattern of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah and Samson's mother.
b: Israel's story repeatedly turns on a woman who could not have children until God stepped in: Sarah (Genesis 18:11), Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), Rachel (Genesis 30:1), Samson's mother (Judges 13:2) and Hannah (1 Samuel 1:2). "Well along in their days" echoes the Greek of Genesis 18:11, where Abraham and Sarah were "far along in years." A reader who knew the Scriptures would expect a child who matters for Israel. The pattern also prepares a contrast: Elizabeth is too old, Mary is too young and unmarried, and God acts in both.

t: Chosen by lot to burn the incense
p: The Mishnah says the incense lot was so prized that a priest could win it only once in his life.
b: Incense was burned on the golden altar inside the sanctuary every morning and every evening (Exodus 30:7–8). According to the Mishnah (compiled about AD 200, describing the temple from memory), the priests of the week's division cast lots each day for the tasks, and the lot for the incense was given only to priests who had never offered it before (Mishnah Tamid 5:2; Yoma 2:4). If that rule held in Zechariah's time, this was the high point of his life as a priest. Luke's readers would see God's hand in the lot (compare Proverbs 16:33; Acts 1:26).

p: Luke uses naos for the holy building itself, and hieron for the whole temple area with its courts.
b: Greek has two words that English Bibles often both translate "temple." Naos is the sanctuary building: the Holy Place, with the lampstand, the table and the incense altar, and the Most Holy Place behind the curtain. Only priests went in. Hieron is the whole complex, including the great outer courts where people gathered, taught and prayed (2:27, 46; 24:53). This site keeps them apart: "sanctuary" for naos (as in Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38) and "temple" for hieron. So Zechariah goes alone into the sanctuary while the crowd prays outside in the courts.

p: Luke does not say which offering. If it was the evening incense, it was the hour when Gabriel came to Daniel and when Judith prayed.
b: The people gathered in the courts while the incense rose inside, praying at the same moment, a picture already found in the Psalms ("Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you," Psalm 141:2). The evening offering, about three in the afternoon, was a regular hour of prayer (Acts 3:1; 10:30). Gabriel last appeared in Scripture "at the time of the evening offering," when Daniel was praying (Daniel 9:21), and Judith prayed at the hour the evening incense was offered in Jerusalem (Judith 9:1). Luke's first scene is Israel at prayer, and God answers.
r: Psalm 141:2; Daniel 9:21; Acts 3:1; Acts 10:30; Judith 9:1; Revelation 8:3–4

p: Angels appear more often in Luke 1–2 than anywhere else in the Gospels.
b: Angelos kyriou, "an angel of the Lord," is the Greek Old Testament's phrase for the messenger through whom God speaks (Genesis 16:7; Judges 13:3). In Luke 1–2 angels announce births, explain them and sing (1:11, 26; 2:9, 13), and then almost disappear from the Gospel until the empty tomb (24:4, 23), framing Jesus' life. The angel stands "to the right" of the incense altar, the side of favor. This angel will name himself as Gabriel (1:19).

p: Zechariah's prayer for a son, or his priestly prayer for Israel's redemption? Probably both.
b: Deēsis is a specific request. The angel's next words, about a son, suggest Zechariah had long asked God for a child, though by now he no longer expects one (1:18). But a priest offering incense on behalf of the people would be praying for Israel, and Jewish prayers of the time asked God to redeem his people. Many interpreters see a deliberate double answer: the private prayer for a son and the public prayer for Israel are answered together, since the son will "turn many Israelites back" (1:16).

p: John means "the LORD has been gracious." Zechariah means "the LORD has remembered."
b: Iōannēs is the Greek form of Hebrew Yehochanan or Yochanan, "the LORD has shown favor" or "has been gracious." Zechariah (Zekharyah) means "the LORD has remembered," and Elizabeth (Elisheva) is usually explained as "my God is an oath" or "my God is fullness." Zechariah's song plays on all three: God shows mercy, remembers his covenant and keeps the oath he swore (1:72–73). The name John breaks with family custom (1:59–63), a sign that this child belongs to a new act of God.

a: Wine and strong drink he must never touch
p: The rule recalls the Nazirite vow, Samson and Samuel. Whether John was a Nazirite is debated.
b: The Nazirite "must keep away from wine and other strong drink" (Numbers 6:3), and Samson's mother was told the same (Judges 13:4–5). The Greek text of 1 Samuel 1:11 adds that Samuel would drink no wine or strong drink. Priests on duty also abstained (Leviticus 10:9). Luke does not mention the uncut hair that marked a Nazirite, so some think John is simply set apart like a priest on permanent duty, or like a prophet; others call him a lifelong Nazirite like Samson and Samuel. Later Jesus contrasts John, who drank no wine, with himself (7:33–34).

a: filled with the Holy Spirit starting in his mother's womb
t: Filled with the Spirit before birth
p: "From the womb" can mean from birth, but 1:41 shows Luke means before it.
b: Eti ek koilias mētros autou can mean "from birth on" (as in Psalm 22:10), but the scene at 1:41, where the unborn John leaps at Mary's greeting, shows that Luke means before birth. Being "filled with the Holy Spirit" is Luke's phrase for the Spirit's power to speak for God (1:41, 67; Acts 2:4; 4:8). From this verse the Western church taught that John was cleansed from original sin before his birth, which is why the church keeps his birthday (June 24) as a feast, as it does only for Jesus and Mary; Ambrose already drew this lesson. Compare Jeremiah 1:5 and Paul in Galatians 1:15.
orig: ἔτι ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς αὐτοῦ (eti ek koilias mētros autou)

p: The angel paraphrases Malachi's promise that Elijah will come back before the LORD's day.
b: Malachi ends the prophets with God's promise to send Elijah before "the great and dreadful day of the LORD," to turn the hearts of fathers to children and children to fathers (Malachi 4:5–6; in Hebrew 3:23–24). Sirach 48:10 repeats the hope. Luke changes the second line: instead of children turning to fathers, the disobedient turn to "the good sense of the righteous." Matthew and Mark say John simply is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12–13; Mark 9:13); Luke says he comes "with Elijah's spirit and power," and leaves out those sayings, while in John 1:21 the Baptist denies being Elijah. Many scholars think Luke also sees Jesus himself in Elijah's role (4:25–26; 7:11–17; 9:54).

p: In 1:16 "the Lord" is Israel's God. Christians soon read John as forerunner of Jesus the Lord.
b: The nearest "Lord" is "the Lord their God" in 1:16, and "ahead of him" in Greek most naturally means ahead of God, as in Malachi 3:1, where the messenger prepares the way before the LORD himself. But in 1:43 Elizabeth calls Mary "my Lord's mother," and in 1:76 Zechariah sings that John will go "ahead of the Lord," in a song about the one born of David's house. Luke lets the word "Lord" slide from God to Jesus, a move that historians of early Christian belief (such as Richard Bauckham and Larry Hurtado) see as a sign of how early Jesus was given the place of Israel's God.

a: How am I to know this?
p: Zechariah asks exactly what Abraham asked. Why is he punished when Mary's question is not?
b: In the Greek Old Testament, Abraham asks in the same words, kata ti gnōsomai: "Lord GOD, how will I know that I will possess it?" (Genesis 15:8). Abraham received a sign; Zechariah receives one too, but it is a sign that silences him. Readers since the church fathers have asked why Mary's question (1:34) is answered gently. A common answer, given by Ambrose and Augustine, is that Zechariah asks for proof that it can happen, while Mary believes it will happen and asks only how; Elizabeth's words in 1:45 ("Blessed is the woman who believed") seem to draw the contrast. Others note that the question itself is not the fault: the angel names his unbelief (1:20).

p: "God is my strong one." Gabriel is named in the Bible only in Daniel and in Luke 1.
b: Gavri'el probably means "God is my strong one" or "man of God." He is one of only two angels named in the Hebrew Bible, both in Daniel: Gabriel explains Daniel's visions (Daniel 8:16) and comes at the hour of the evening offering to reveal the seventy weeks (Daniel 9:21–27). Michael is the other. Later Jewish writings list Gabriel among the archangels who stand before God (1 Enoch 20:7; 40:9), and Raphael in Tobit 12:15 calls himself one of seven angels who stand ready before the Lord. "The one who stands before God" marks him as a courtier of the highest rank. Luke may intend the echo of Daniel's promise of an end to sin and "everlasting righteousness" (Daniel 9:24).

a: to give you the good news
p: Luke's first use of the verb behind "evangelize." He prefers the verb; Mark and Matthew, the noun.
b: Euangelisasthai is the verb form of euangelion, "good news." Mark and Matthew mostly use the noun; Luke never uses the noun in his Gospel, but uses the verb ten times (2:10; 3:18; 4:18, 43) and Acts many more. Its background is the herald of Isaiah who brings good news of God's return (Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 61:1). The first good news in Luke is the birth of a child to an old priest.

a: you will go silent and lose the power to speak
p: Zechariah cannot give the blessing the people wait for. The Gospel ends with Jesus blessing them.
b: When the incense was finished, the priests came out to bless the people with the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26 (Mishnah Tamid 7:2 describes this). Zechariah comes out and cannot speak (1:22), so the blessing is left unspoken. Many commentators note that Luke's Gospel ends with the matching scene: Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his followers, who return to the temple praising God (24:50–53). The silence is also a sign, as Daniel fell speechless after his vision (Daniel 10:15) and Ezekiel was made mute (Ezekiel 3:26), until the promised word comes true (1:64).

p: Kōphos can mean unable to speak, unable to hear, or both. 1:62 suggests both.
b: Kōphos means "blunted," and is used of those who cannot speak (11:14), cannot hear (7:22), or both. At 1:62 people make signs to Zechariah to ask about the name, which they would hardly need to do if he could hear, so many readers think Luke pictures him as deaf as well as mute. Others think the signs were simply natural with someone who could not answer aloud.

a: She hid herself away for five months
p: Luke does not say. The hiding keeps the secret until the "sixth month" reveal to Mary.
b: Suggestions: modesty in pregnancy at her age; waiting until no one could doubt it; a time of thanksgiving apart; or, as Origen and Ambrose suggested, shame at conceiving so late. In the story's design, the hiding means no one knows about the pregnancy until Gabriel tells Mary in the sixth month (1:26, 36), so Elizabeth's pregnancy becomes a sign given to Mary alone.

a: to take away my disgrace among people
p: Elizabeth echoes Rachel: "God has taken away my disgrace."
b: When Rachel finally bore Joseph she said, "God has taken away my disgrace" (Genesis 30:23); the Greek of both verses uses oneidos, "reproach, disgrace." In a world where a family's future depended on children, barrenness was often treated as a sign of God's displeasure and a matter of public shame (1 Samuel 1:6). Luke has already told readers that Elizabeth was righteous (1:6), so the shame was undeserved. "Looked my way" echoes God looking on Hannah's misery (1 Samuel 1:11).

p: Elizabeth's pregnancy (1:24, 36), not a month of the year. The church calendar is built on it.
b: The count is from Elizabeth's conception: she hid five months (1:24), and Mary is told it is Elizabeth's sixth month (1:36). The church calendar later counted from this: the Annunciation on March 25, nine months before Christmas, and John's birth on June 24, three months after the Annunciation and six months before Christmas. The calendar dates are church tradition, not something Luke states. The two announcements, Gabriel to Zechariah and Gabriel to Mary, are told as matching panels, with Mary's always a step higher (see the chapter page).
orig: ἐν δὲ τῷ μηνὶ τῷ ἕκτῳ (en de tō mēni tō hektō)

a: a Galilean town by the name of Nazareth
p: A small farming village, never named in the Old Testament, Josephus or early rabbinic writings.
b: Luke calls Nazareth a polis, "town," but it was a village of perhaps a few hundred people in the hills of Lower Galilee, about four miles from the rebuilt city of Sepphoris. Excavations have found first-century houses, tombs and terraces; in 2009 the Israel Antiquities Authority reported a house of Jesus' time near the Church of the Annunciation. The contrast is deliberate: the first announcement came in Jerusalem's sanctuary to a priest; the second comes in an obscure Galilean village to a young woman with no title.

a: a virgin who was promised in marriage
p: Jewish betrothal was a binding legal bond. The couple married, but lived apart for a time.
b: Emnēsteumenēn means "betrothed." In Jewish custom a betrothal (later called erusin or kiddushin) was a legal marriage contract: it could be ended only by divorce, and the man could be called the woman's husband (Matthew 1:19). The bride usually stayed in her father's house for up to a year before the wedding and the move to her husband's home. Girls were often betrothed young, commonly in their early teens, though we do not know Mary's age. Parthenos means a young unmarried woman and, as 1:34 makes clear, here a virgin. The words "virgin," "house of David," "conceive," "son" and "his name" in 1:27–31 echo the Greek of Isaiah 7:13–14, though Luke, unlike Matthew 1:23, does not quote it.

t: Is Joseph or Mary "of David's house"?
p: The phrase most naturally goes with Joseph. Early tradition also made Mary a descendant of David.
b: The Greek order puts "of the house of David" right after "Joseph," and 2:4 says plainly that Joseph was "of David's house and clan." Jesus is legally David's son through Joseph, who names him (as in Matthew 1:20–25). Some early Christians (Ignatius, Justin, the Protevangelium of James) also said Mary was of David's line, and some read 1:27 that way; others note that Elizabeth, Mary's relative, was of Aaron's family (1:5, 36). Luke himself is concerned with Joseph's line, since his genealogy of Jesus runs through Joseph (3:23–31).

p: Chaire was the ordinary Greek hello, but it literally means "Rejoice," as in the prophets' calls to Zion.
b: Chaire was the everyday greeting (Matthew 26:49; 28:9), as "hello" or "peace" would be. Its root meaning is "rejoice," and in the Greek Old Testament the same imperative opens prophecies to the "daughter of Zion": "Rejoice, daughter of Zion ... the Lord is in your midst" (Zephaniah 3:14–17; compare Joel 2:21; Zechariah 9:9). Stanislas Lyonnet and René Laurentin argued that Luke means this echo, presenting Mary as Daughter Zion, Israel waiting for its king. Raymond Brown and many others doubt it, since Luke uses chaire simply as a greeting elsewhere. The Plain uses "Greetings"; the Orthodox liturgy sings "Rejoice" (Chaire) to Mary in the Akathist Hymn.

a: you who have been shown favor
p: The Greek says God has graced or favored her. The Latin "full of grace" comes from the Vulgate.
b: Kecharitōmenē is a perfect passive participle of charitoō, "to give grace or favor." It describes Mary by what God has done for her, and the perfect tense points to a favor already given that lasts. The only other New Testament use is Ephesians 1:6, of the grace God "freely gave" all believers in his Son. Jerome's Latin Vulgate translated it gratia plena, "full of grace," which passed into the Hail Mary and the Douay-Rheims Bible; the Greek "full of grace" (plērēs charitos) is used of Jesus (John 1:14) and Stephen (Acts 6:8), not here. Catholic teaching reads the perfect participle as a fullness of grace that included Mary's freedom from sin from her conception; Protestant readers, following Erasmus and Calvin, take it as God's free favor, which is the theme of 1:30. Most modern translations, Catholic ones included, say "favored one." See the card on the chapter page.

p: The words Gideon heard before being sent to save Israel: a promise of help for a task.
b: "The LORD is with you, you mighty fighter," the angel told Gideon (Judges 6:12), before sending him against Midian; Boaz greets his workers in the same words (Ruth 2:4). In the Bible the phrase usually comes with a calling: God will be present to help with a hard task (Exodus 3:12; Jeremiah 1:8). Mary's calling is to bear a son who will reign.

a: You have found favor with God
p: An Old Testament phrase for being chosen by God's free kindness, as Noah and Moses were.
b: "To find favor" (heurein charin) translates the Hebrew matsa chen: Noah "found favor in the LORD's eyes" (Genesis 6:8), and so did Moses (Exodus 33:12–17). The word charis here is the same root as the angel's greeting in 1:28, which explains it: Mary is "favored" because God has chosen to show her favor. Luke uses charis again of the child Jesus (2:40, 52).

p: Yeshua, "the LORD saves." Here Mary names him; in Matthew, Joseph does, with the same words.
b: Iēsous is the Greek form of Yeshua (a short form of Yehoshua, Joshua), "the LORD saves," a common Jewish name. Matthew explains the meaning (Matthew 1:21); Luke does not, though "Savior" and "salvation" fill these chapters (1:47, 69, 71, 77; 2:11, 30). In Luke the angel tells Mary, "Name him Jesus"; in Matthew the angel tells Joseph the same, in the same Greek words (Matthew 1:21). The pattern of the announcement (you will conceive, bear a son, call his name) follows Old Testament birth announcements: Hagar (Genesis 16:11), Samson's mother (Judges 13:3) and Isaiah 7:14.

a: will be called Son of the Most High
t: Son of the Most High, and a scroll from Qumran
p: An Aramaic fragment from Qumran speaks of one called "son of God" and "son of the Most High."
b: "The Most High" (Hypsistos, Hebrew Elyon) is a title of God Luke likes (1:35, 76; 6:35; 8:28; Acts 7:48). A damaged Aramaic text from Qumran Cave 4, the Aramaic Apocalypse (4Q246), copied before Jesus' time, says of a coming figure that he "will be called son of God" and "son of the Most High," and speaks of an everlasting kingdom. The match with 1:32–35, where Jesus "will be called Son of the Most High" and "will be called holy, God's Son," is striking and shows that this language was at home in Jewish hopes before Christianity. Scholars disagree whether the Qumran figure is a messianic king or an arrogant ruler claiming divine titles. Either way, the titles here first mean Israel's king, God's son by adoption (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7); 1:35 will give "God's Son" a deeper ground.

a: the throne of David his father
p: The angel repeats God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7: a son, a throne, a kingdom forever.
b: Through the prophet Nathan God promised David an heir whose throne would last: "Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:16), and "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14). Isaiah promised a son on "David's throne" whose rule would have no end (Isaiah 9:7). Luke's angel draws all of this into two verses: great, Son of the Most High, David's throne, reigning over Jacob's house, a kingdom without end. "His father" means ancestor. Acts later claims the promise was fulfilled when God raised Jesus and seated him at his right hand (Acts 2:30–36).
r: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:6–7; Psalm 89:3–4; Psalm 132:11; Acts 2:30–36; Acts 13:22–23

a: His kingdom will have no end
t: "His kingdom will have no end" in the Creed
p: The church put this line into the Nicene Creed against a teacher who said Christ's reign would end.
b: The phrase echoes Daniel 7:14, where the "one like a son of man" receives a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and Micah 4:7. In the 300s Marcellus of Ancyra taught, from 1 Corinthians 15:24–28, that the Son's kingdom would end when he handed it over to the Father. The creed of the Council of Constantinople (381), the form of the Nicene Creed most churches say today, added the words "his kingdom will have no end," taken from this verse. Luke's angel speaks of a Davidic king; the church read it as the eternal reign of the Son.

a: since I do not know a man
t: "I do not know a man": why ask?
p: Mary is betrothed. Why is she puzzled? Three answers: plain sense, a vow, or the story's design.
b: "Know" is the biblical word for sexual union (Genesis 4:1; Matthew 1:25). The puzzle is that Mary is betrothed; a reader might expect her to assume the child would come once she and Joseph lived together. (1) Plain reading: she means "I am a virgin," and she hears the angel speaking of a conception now, before the wedding. (2) Vow reading: Gregory of Nyssa (Sermon on the Nativity) and Augustine (On Holy Virginity 4) took the present tense, "I do not know a man," to mean she had resolved to stay a virgin, as the Protevangelium of James also imagines; this reading supports Catholic and Orthodox belief in Mary's lasting virginity. (3) Literary reading (Raymond Brown and many others): the question is a storyteller's device that lets the angel explain the virginal conception in 1:35. Many hold (1) and (3) together.
orig: ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (epei andra ou ginōskō)

a: will cast its shadow over you
p: The same verb is used of God's cloud covering the tabernacle and the mountain of transfiguration.
b: Episkiazō, "to overshadow," is used in the Greek Old Testament when the cloud of God's glory settled on the tent of meeting, so that Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:35), and in Luke when the cloud covers Jesus and the disciples on the mountain (9:34). It is also used of God's protecting shade (Psalm 91:4). Nothing in the word is sexual: Mary's conception is pictured as God's creative presence coming down, as the Spirit "hovered" over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). The same words, "the Holy Spirit will come upon you" (Acts 1:8), are Jesus' promise to his followers before Pentecost.

a: the one being born will be called holy, God's Son
t: Two ways to read the last line
p: "The holy one born will be called God's Son," or "the child born will be called holy, God's Son."
b: The Greek to gennōmenon hagion klēthēsetai, huios theou can be punctuated two ways: "the one being born, holy, will be called Son of God," or "the one being born will be called holy, Son of God." Both are grammatical and the sense is close. What matters more is the "For that reason": the child is God's Son because of how he comes to be, through the Spirit and the Most High's power. That goes beyond 1:32, where "Son of the Most High" could mean a king adopted by God. Luke does not explain how this relates to Jesus' existence before his birth, which John 1:1–14 teaches; the creeds later joined the two.
orig: τὸ γεννώμενον ἅγιον κληθήσεται υἱὸς θεοῦ

t: Sons of gods in the ancient world
p: Greek and Roman stories told of rulers fathered by gods. Luke's story is different in kind.
b: Ancient readers knew stories of great men conceived by gods: Plutarch reports a tale that Alexander the Great was fathered by Zeus, and Suetonius (Augustus 94) tells a story that Augustus' mother conceived him by the god Apollo in the form of a snake. Some critics argued that Christians borrowed such legends; Justin Martyr already answered pagans who compared them (First Apology 21–22, 33). The differences are large: in the Greek stories a god takes a woman's body as a male partner, while in Luke there is no union, only God's Spirit and power creating life in a virgin who consents. The closer background is Jewish: God's word that creates and the miraculous births to barren women. The story's Jewish setting and its restraint make direct borrowing unlikely, though Luke's Gentile readers would surely hear the contrast with the emperor's claims (see 2:1, 11).

p: Luke does not say how. The link joins a priestly family to a Galilean one.
b: Syngenis means "kinswoman," any relative. Elizabeth is of Aaron's line (1:5) and Mary is betrothed to a man of David's line. Some early writers drew from this that Mary was of both priestly and royal descent, which would make Jesus both king and priest; Luke does not say so. The kinship explains why Mary goes to Elizabeth, and it ties John and Jesus together from before their births.

p: The angel's last words answer the question God asked Abraham and Sarah in Genesis 18:14.
b: When Sarah laughed at the promise of a son in her old age, God asked, "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:14). The Greek Old Testament translates "anything" as rhēma, "word" or "thing," and "too wonderful" as "impossible": "Is any word impossible with God?" Luke's angel answers that question with the same two words. Rhēma means both "word" and "matter," as Hebrew davar does, so the sense is both "nothing is impossible for God" and "nothing God says will fail." Mary answers in the next verse with the same word: "just as you have said" (literally "according to your word").

p: Doulē means a female slave. Many Bibles soften it to "servant"; this site keeps "slave."
b: Doulē is a slave woman. In the Greek Old Testament it is the humble word a woman uses of herself before God or a great man, as Hannah does: "look at the misery of your servant" (1 Samuel 1:11, where the Greek is doulē). Many English Bibles say "servant" or "handmaid," because in English "slave" sounds only like ownership and cruelty, and Greek and Roman slavery was indeed harsh. But doulos also described those who belonged wholly to a king or a god, and "slave of God" was a title of honor for Moses and the prophets. This site translates the word "slave" throughout and notes it at first use in each book.

a: May it be done to me just as you have said
p: The Fiat. Irenaeus made Mary's obedience the undoing of Eve's disobedience.
b: In Latin the words begin fiat mihi, "let it be done to me," and they are often called Mary's Fiat. Luke stresses that Mary agrees: the angel waits for her answer, and the scene ends only when she gives it. Irenaeus (about AD 180, Against Heresies 3.22.4) contrasted her with Eve: the knot Eve's disobedience tied, Mary's faith untied. Catholic teaching sees Mary freely cooperating in salvation (Lumen Gentium 56); the Orthodox honor her as the Theotokos who gave her consent for the whole human race. Protestant readers, such as Luther in his commentary on the Magnificat, praise her as a model believer who simply trusted God's word, while denying that her consent added anything to Christ's saving work.

p: Luke does not name it. Since the Byzantine period tradition has pointed to Ein Karem near Jerusalem.
b: "The hills" (oreinē) is the hill country of Judea (1:65). Priests lived in towns around Jerusalem when they were not on duty. The town is unnamed. Christian tradition, at least from the Byzantine period, has placed Zechariah's home at Ein Karem, about four miles west of Jerusalem, where churches of the Visitation and of John's birth stand today; earlier guesses included Hebron or Juttah, priestly towns (Joshua 21:11, 16). The journey from Nazareth would have taken several days.

a: the baby in her womb leaped
p: The verb recalls Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah's womb, here turned to joy.
b: Eskirtēsen, "leaped, skipped," is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when Jacob and Esau "crushed against each other" in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25:22), a sign of the older serving the younger. Here the older child greets the younger with joy (1:44). Malachi 4:2 uses it of calves leaping out of the stall. Luke presents John's first act as witness to Jesus, before either is born; Origen and Ambrose said John prophesied from the womb. The word brephos is used of the unborn John here and of the newborn Jesus in 2:12, 16; some modern Christians cite this in debates about the unborn, while others note that Luke is not addressing that question.

p: Elizabeth blesses Mary as Deborah blessed Jael and Uzziah blessed Judith: women who saved Israel.
b: "Among women" is a Hebrew way to say "most blessed of all women." Deborah sang, "Blessed above women be Jael" (Judges 5:24), after Jael killed Sisera, and Uzziah told Judith, "you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth!" (Judith 13:18), after she killed Holofernes. Both women saved Israel from an enemy. Mary's blessing comes not from a victory but from the child she carries, which Elizabeth names in the next breath. The angel's greeting (1:28) and Elizabeth's words together make the first half of the Hail Mary, the Ave Maria, a prayer formed in this way by the 1000s; see the card on the chapter page.

a: the fruit of your womb is blessed
p: A blessing from the covenant, with an echo of God's oath to put David's offspring on his throne.
b: "The fruit of your womb will be blessed" (Deuteronomy 28:4) is among the blessings God promises Israel for obedience. In Psalm 132:11, God swears to David, "From the fruit of your body / I will set one on your throne" (Psalm 132:11, the Greek has "womb"), the promise the angel has just repeated (1:32). Elizabeth blesses the child before he is born, and before anyone has told her about him.

t: "My Lord's mother" and the title Theotokos
p: Elizabeth calls the unborn Jesus "my Lord." The church later called Mary Theotokos, "God-bearer."
b: Elizabeth uses "Lord" (kyrios), the word Luke uses for God in 1:6–46, for Mary's unborn child. In the Psalms "my lord" can be the king (Psalm 110:1), and Luke may mean the Messiah; but Luke's readers would also hear the divine sense (see the note on 1:17). In 431 the Council of Ephesus approved the title Theotokos, "the one who gave birth to God," for Mary, against Nestorius, who preferred "Christ-bearer." The point was about Christ: the child Mary bore was truly God. Catholics, Orthodox and the Protestant Reformers (Luther explicitly, Calvin with caution about the phrase "Mother of God") accepted the council's teaching.

t: The ark comes to the hill country
p: Luke's scene seems to echo David bringing the ark toward Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 6.
b: When David brought the ark of the covenant from the hill country of Judah, he asked, "How can I ever have the LORD's ark come to me?" (2 Samuel 6:9). The ark stayed three months in the house of Obed-edom, who was blessed (2 Samuel 6:11), and David danced before it with shouts of joy (2 Samuel 6:14–16). Luke's scene has a journey into the hill country of Judah, the question "How does this happen to me, that my Lord's mother comes to me?", a leap of joy, a loud cry and a stay of about three months (1:56). René Laurentin and others see Mary pictured as the ark carrying God's presence; Raymond Brown thought the echoes too loose to be sure. The 2 Samuel 6 card on this site gives the churches' views.

a: Blessed is the woman who believed
p: In 1:42 Mary is "blessed" by God (eulogēmenē); here she is "happy, fortunate" (makaria) because she believed.
b: English has one word where Greek has two. Eulogēmenē (1:42) means "spoken well of, blessed by God." Makaria here is the word of the Beatitudes (6:20–22): fortunate, to be congratulated. Elizabeth praises Mary first for whom she carries, then for her faith, which contrasts with Zechariah's unbelief (1:20). Luke returns to this when a woman calls Jesus' mother blessed and Jesus answers that those who hear God's word and keep it are the blessed ones (11:27–28): Mary, who heard and believed, is both. The Greek can also be read "Blessed is she who believed, because what the Lord told her will be carried out," as the KJV takes it.

a: My soul declares how great the Lord is
p: The Latin first word of Mary's song, "magnifies," gave it its name.
b: Megalynei means "makes great" or "declares great"; Latin Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Mary cannot make God greater; she makes his greatness known, as a psalm calls, "Make the LORD great with me" (Psalm 34:3). "Soul" and "spirit" in 1:46–47 are not two parts of Mary but Hebrew parallelism: "my soul ... my spirit" both mean "I, my whole self." The song opens as Hannah's does: "My heart leaps for joy in the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:1). The song falls into two halves: what God has done for Mary (1:46–50) and what he has done for Israel (1:51–55).
orig: Μεγαλύνει ἡ ψυχή μου τὸν κύριον (Megalynei hē psychē mou ton kyrion)

p: Mary calls God "my Savior." The churches read this line differently.
b: "God my Savior" echoes Psalms such as Psalm 25:5 and Habakkuk 3:18 in the Greek. Protestant interpreters often point to this line as proof that Mary was a sinner who needed saving, like everyone else. Catholic teaching agrees that Mary needed a Savior, but holds that she was saved in a unique way: preserved from original sin from her conception "in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior" (Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 1854). The Orthodox say Mary was cleansed and made all-holy by the Spirit, especially at the Annunciation, without the Catholic dogma. The 1:28 card on the chapter page sets the views side by side.

p: Mary uses almost the same Greek words as Hannah's prayer: the "lowliness" or "misery" of God's slave.
b: Hannah prayed, "if you will really look at the misery of your servant" (1 Samuel 1:11), and in the Greek the phrase is epiblepsēs epi tēn tapeinōsin tēs doulēs sou, nearly word for word Mary's line. Tapeinōsis means a low condition: poverty, humiliation, low status, not first the virtue of humility. Mary is a young woman from a village, without rank, and soon pregnant before her wedding. God's choice of the lowly is the theme the second half of the song turns into a rule of his kingdom (1:52).
orig: τὴν ταπείνωσιν τῆς δούλης αὐτοῦ (tēn tapeinōsin tēs doulēs autou)

a: every generation will count me blessed
p: Leah said women would call her happy. Mary says every generation will.
b: When Leah's maid bore a son, Leah said, "Happy me! For daughters will call me happy" (Genesis 30:13); the Greek uses the same verb, makarizō. Mary's claim is larger: every generation. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see their honor of Mary as fulfilling this verse (Catechism 971). Luther, in his commentary on the Magnificat, also urged Christians to call her blessed, while insisting the praise belongs to the grace of God shown in her rather than to her own worth. See the card on the chapter page.

a: the Mighty One has worked great things for me
p: Language of God the warrior who saves, from Zephaniah and Deuteronomy.
b: "The Mighty One" (ho dynatos) recalls God as the warrior who saves in Zephaniah 3:17 ("a warrior who rescues") and Psalm 24:8. "Great things" is what Moses told Israel God had done for them in the exodus (Deuteronomy 10:21). The line ends with a psalm's praise: "His name is holy and to be feared" (Psalm 111:9). The personal "for me" turns into a statement about God's character that holds for every generation (1:50).

p: Greek eleos translates Hebrew hesed, God's faithful covenant love.
b: In the Greek Old Testament eleos usually translates hesed, the loyal, faithful love God shows within his covenant, which this site renders "loyal love" in the Old Testament. The line echoes Psalm 103:17: "the loyal love of the LORD rests on those who fear him" (Psalm 103:17). "Mercy" is one of the key words of Luke 1, used five times (1:50, 54, 58, 72, 78): God remembers his covenant love for Israel.

a: He has used the strength of his arm
p: God "has" scattered the proud and pulled down rulers. Has this happened, or is it promised?
b: The verbs in 1:51–55 are Greek aorists, normally past. Readers explain them as: (1) a summary of what God did in Israel's history, at the exodus with "a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 4:34; Psalm 89:10); (2) a "prophetic past," speaking of a sure future as already done, as Hebrew prophets did; (3) a description of what God always does (some grammarians call it "gnomic"); (4) praise for what God has begun by choosing Mary, with the rest sure to follow. Many interpreters combine (2) and (4): in the conception of the Messiah, the reversal of the world's order has begun.

a: He has pulled rulers down from thrones
p: The God who lifts the lowly and brings down the mighty: a theme that runs through Luke.
b: The line echoes Hannah: "he puts them down, and he also raises them up" (1 Samuel 2:7), and Psalm 113:7–8. In Luke the reversal returns in the blessings and woes (6:20–26), the rich man and Lazarus (16:19–31), the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14) and the saying that the exalted will be humbled (14:11). Readers differ over how political it is. Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez read it as God's commitment to the poor and against oppressive power; Dietrich Bonhoeffer, preaching in London in Advent 1933, months after the Nazis took power in Germany, called it a passionate and even revolutionary song. Others stress that the song is about God's action, not a call to human revolt, and that Luke's "lowly" are those who depend on God. Most agree that the material sense, real hunger and real thrones, cannot be spiritualized away.

a: The hungry he has loaded with good things
p: Psalm 107 and Hannah's song both speak of God feeding the hungry.
b: The psalm says God "filled up the hungry soul with good" (Psalm 107:9), and Hannah sang that "the hungry stop being hungry" (1 Samuel 2:5). Luke will later have Jesus bless the hungry and warn the full (6:21, 25) and feed five thousand (9:17). The rich sent away "with empty hands" anticipates the rich ruler who goes away sad (18:23) and the rich man in Hades (16:25).

a: He has taken hold of Israel, his servant, to help him
p: Isaiah's picture of God grasping his servant Israel by the hand.
b: Antelabeto means "took hold of, came to the help of." In Isaiah 41:8–9 God calls Israel "my servant" and says "it was you I grasped from the ends of the earth" (Isaiah 41:9); the Greek uses the same verb. The song ends not with Mary but with Israel: her child is God's help to his whole people. "Servant" here is pais, the word for Isaiah's servant figure (Isaiah 42:1).
orig: ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ (antelabeto Israēl paidos autou)

a: to Abraham and his offspring for all time
p: The song ends with God's promise to Abraham's offspring, a promise Luke does not take back.
b: God's promise to Abraham and his offspring (Genesis 17:7; 22:17–18) is the ground of Israel's hope, and it frames Luke 1 (1:55, 73). Micah's prayer ends the same way: "You will give faithfulness to Jacob, loyal love to Abraham, as you swore to our ancestors" (Micah 7:20). For Luke the promise is for "Abraham and his offspring for all time": he presents Jesus as the fulfillment of God's faithfulness to Israel, not its replacement. How the church relates to that promise is debated (see the topic The Church and Israel), but in this song the beneficiary is plainly Israel.

t: Did Mary stay for the birth?
p: Three months would bring Elizabeth to term. Luke tells Mary's departure first, then the birth.
b: Elizabeth was six months pregnant when Mary arrived (1:36), so three months brings her close to delivery. Luke says Mary went home, then tells of John's birth (1:57). Some readers think Mary left just before; others, including many church fathers, assumed she stayed to help and Luke simply finished her part of the story first, as he often closes one scene before opening the next. The "three months" may also echo the ark's three months in the house of Obed-edom (2 Samuel 6:11).

a: had made his mercy great toward her
p: The same verb as Mary's "magnifies" in 1:46.
b: Emegalynen is the verb Mary used in 1:46: Mary makes the Lord great, and the Lord has made his mercy great to Elizabeth. The neighbors say what Mary's song said: God's mercy has reached a humble woman. The phrase echoes Lot's thanks in Genesis 19:19 in the Greek.
orig: ἐμεγάλυνεν... τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ (emegalynen... to eleos autou)

a: they arrived to circumcise the boy
p: John is circumcised as the law commands. Naming at circumcision is first attested here.
b: The law commands circumcision on the eighth day: "Every male among you, generation after generation, is to be circumcised at eight days old" (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). In the Old Testament babies are named at birth; this is the earliest evidence for naming a boy at his circumcision, as Jews do today at the brit milah. Jesus too will be circumcised and named on the eighth day (2:21). Luke shows both families keeping the law faithfully.

a: they started calling him Zechariah, his father's name
p: Relatives expected a family name. "John" broke the pattern.
b: The imperfect verb (ekaloun) means "they were trying to call him." Jewish families of the period often reused names within the family, especially the grandfather's; naming a son after his living father is attested but less common. Either way, relatives and neighbors had a say in naming a child, and a name from outside the family surprised them (1:61). Elizabeth and Zechariah, independently, insist on the name the angel gave (1:13), and the agreement is itself a small sign.

p: Zechariah does not choose a name; he states a fact. His obedience ends his silence.
b: Zechariah writes in the present tense: the name is already given by God (1:13), and he only confirms it. The "small tablet" (pinakidion) was probably a wooden board covered with wax for writing with a stylus. Once he obeys the angel's word, his mouth is opened (1:64), which ties his silence to his earlier unbelief (1:20). Ancient preachers made this a lesson that faith restores what doubt takes away.

p: His first words are a blessing: the song that follows begins "Blessed is the Lord."
b: Eulogōn, "blessing," is the Jewish way to praise God: a berakhah, a prayer beginning "Blessed are you, LORD." The priest who could not bless the people at the start (1:22) now blesses God, and Luke gives the words in 1:68–79, which begin with that formula. The Greek says literally that his mouth was opened "and his tongue," leaving the second verb ("set free") to be understood.

a: the hand of the Lord was with him
p: An Old Testament phrase for God's power at work in a person, used of prophets such as Elijah.
b: "The hand of the LORD" was on Elijah when he outran Ahab's chariot (1 Kings 18:46) and on Ezekiel when he saw visions (Ezekiel 1:3); in Acts it is with the believers in Antioch (Acts 11:21). The sentence can be read as Luke's own comment ("And indeed..."), as here, following the oldest manuscripts that have "for" (gar), or as part of what the people said, as in the Byzantine text without "for." See the variant.

p: Many Jews believed prophecy had ceased after Malachi. Luke 1–2 is full of it.
b: A common Jewish belief of the time held that prophecy had stopped after the last prophets. 1 Maccabees speaks of distress "worse than any since the day a prophet was last seen among them" (1 Maccabees 9:27), and a later rabbinic tradition says the holy spirit departed from Israel when Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died (Tosefta Sotah 13:3). Others at Qumran and elsewhere claimed prophetic insight, so the belief was not universal. In Luke 1–2 the Spirit fills Elizabeth, Zechariah and Simeon, and Anna is a prophetess (1:41, 67; 2:25–27, 36): the long silence is over. Joel's promise that God's slaves, men and women, would prophesy (Acts 2:17–18) begins here.

a: Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel
p: Zechariah opens with the blessing that closes books of the Psalms. The Latin is Benedictus.
b: "Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel" closes the first, fourth and fifth books of the Psalms (Psalm 41:13; 72:18; 106:48), and David used it when Solomon was made king (1 Kings 1:48). The Latin Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel gives the song its name. The song falls into two parts: praise for the salvation God has raised up in David's house (1:68–75), and words to the infant John about his part in it (1:76–79). Notice that the Davidic "horn" is not John, who is of priestly descent, but the child Mary carries.

p: Episkeptomai is the Bible's word for God coming to see to his people's need, to rescue or to judge.
b: When God "visits" (Hebrew paqad, Greek episkeptomai) in the Old Testament, he comes to act: Joseph promised that "God will surely come to help you" (Genesis 50:24) and bring Israel out of Egypt, and Naomi heard "that the LORD had come to help his people by giving them bread" (Ruth 1:6). The word brackets the song (1:68, 78). Later the crowd at Nain says "God has visited his people" (7:16), and Jesus weeps over Jerusalem because it did not recognize the season when God came to visit it (19:44).

p: The hope of a people under foreign rule. Luke's story keeps asking what kind of redemption it is.
b: Lytrōsis, "redemption," was a word of national hope: the coins of the Jewish revolts against Rome were stamped with slogans such as "for the redemption of Zion" and "freedom of Zion." The psalm says God "sent his people redemption" (Psalm 111:9). Anna speaks to those looking for Jerusalem's redemption (2:38), and after the crucifixion two disciples confess that they had hoped he would be the one to redeem Israel (24:21). Luke lets this hope stand and then reshapes it around the cross and resurrection; whether the political hope is fulfilled, postponed or transformed is a question Acts 1:6 asks again.

p: A horn is a picture of strength, from a bull or ram. Here it means a mighty king who saves.
b: An animal's horn was a picture of strength and victory: Hannah sang "my horn is raised high by the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:1), and David called God "the horn that saves me" (Psalm 18:2; compare 2 Samuel 22:3). Above all Psalm 132:17: "There I will make a horn spring up for David" (Psalm 132:17), with the next line about God's "anointed one." Zechariah's line takes that promise as fulfilled "in the house of David": the horn is the Messiah, Mary's son.
r: 1 Samuel 2:1; 1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 18:2; 2 Samuel 22:3; Psalm 132:17; Ezekiel 29:21

p: The song uses the language of national rescue. How does Luke's story fulfill it?
b: The words echo the psalm of Israel's rescue at the Sea: "He rescued them from the grip of the one who hated them" (Psalm 106:10). Spoken in Herod's day under Rome, they would sound political. Readers take them in different ways: (1) Luke means real rescue from oppressors, partly fulfilled and partly still awaited (compare 21:28; Acts 1:6–7); (2) the enemies are reinterpreted as sin, Satan and death, as 1:77 already hints ("by having their sins forgiven"); (3) Luke's story is tragic: Jerusalem did not recognize its visitation, and enemies surrounded it (19:43–44). Many scholars think Luke wants all three heard, and that the song's original hope is honestly left in tension with what follows.

a: calling to mind his holy covenant
p: Zechariah means "the LORD remembers." The song says God remembered and kept his oath.
b: Commentators have long noticed that the song echoes the three names in the story. Zechariah (Zekhar-yah) means "the LORD has remembered," and God "remembers" his covenant here (1:72). Elizabeth (Eli-sheva) can mean "my God has sworn," and the next line speaks of the "oath he swore" (1:73). John (Yo-chanan) means "the LORD has shown favor," and the song speaks of "mercy" (1:72, 78). Whether Luke or his sources intended the wordplay cannot be known, but Hebrew-speaking hearers would catch it.
orig: μνησθῆναι διαθήκης ἁγίας αὐτοῦ (mnēsthēnai diathēkēs hagias autou)

a: the oath he swore to Abraham our father
p: After the binding of Isaac, God swore by himself to bless Abraham's offspring.
b: The oath is the one sworn after Abraham offered Isaac: "By myself I swear, says the LORD" (Genesis 22:16), with the promise that Abraham's offspring "will take over the gate of his enemies" (Genesis 22:17). That may explain why rescue from enemies follows (1:74). Luke's readers knew that the same promise said all the nations would be blessed in Abraham's offspring (Genesis 22:18; Acts 3:25).

a: we would worship him with nothing to fear
p: The goal of rescue is worship, as at the exodus: "Let my people go, so that they may serve me."
b: Latreuein is to serve God in worship; Anna "served" God night and day (2:37) with the same verb. At the exodus Moses demanded that Pharaoh let Israel go to serve (that is, worship) God (Exodus 7:16; 8:1). Zechariah, a priest, hopes for a people free to worship without fear, "in holiness and righteousness," for all their days.

t: The song turns to the baby
p: Zechariah speaks to the eight-day-old John: a prophet of the Most High.
b: The address kai sy de, paidion marks the turn: after praising God for the Davidic Savior (1:68–75), the father speaks to his own son. Jesus will be "Son of the Most High" (1:32); John will be "a prophet of the Most High." The difference in title shows the order Luke keeps throughout: John is great (1:15), but Jesus is greater. Jesus later calls John "more than a prophet" (7:26–28).

p: Malachi's messenger and Isaiah's voice in the wilderness. Luke quotes Isaiah at 3:4.
b: This combines Malachi 3:1 ("I am about to send my messenger, and he will clear a road before me") and Isaiah 40:3: "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3). Luke quotes the Isaiah passage in full when John begins preaching (3:4–6), and Jesus applies the Malachi text to John (7:27). Mark joined the two at the start of his Gospel (Mark 1:2–3), where the site renders hodos "road," as here.

p: Luke defines salvation as the forgiveness of sins, the heart of John's and the apostles' preaching.
b: Aphesis hamartiōn, "release of sins," is a key phrase in Luke-Acts: John preaches a baptism of repentance for it (3:3), the risen Jesus commands it to be preached to all nations (24:47), and Peter promises it in Jesus' name (Acts 2:38; 10:43). Aphesis also means "release" or "freedom," as in Jesus' reading from Isaiah: "release for the captives" (4:18). In this song political rescue (1:71) and forgiveness (1:77) stand side by side.
orig: ἐν ἀφέσει ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν (en aphesei hamartiōn autōn)

p: Anatolē means the rising of the sun, but in the Greek Old Testament it also names the messianic "Branch."
b: Anatolē is the "rising" of a heavenly body, hence sunrise or the east (the magi's star seen "at its rising," Matthew 2:2). It is also the Greek Old Testament's word for the coming "Branch" or "Shoot" of David (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12, where the Greek says "Anatolē is his name"). Here the light and the shining (1:79) favor "dawn," and Malachi 4:2 promises that "a sun of righteousness will rise." Numbers 24:17 (a star will "rise" from Jacob) uses the same verb. Many think Luke means both: the Davidic Shoot pictured as the rising sun. The church's Advent hymn "O Oriens" ("O Dayspring") draws on this verse.
r: Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; Malachi 4:2; Numbers 24:17; Isaiah 60:1–3; Matthew 2:2

a: people sitting in the dark, in death's shadow
p: Isaiah's promise of light for the people in deep shadow, which Matthew applies to Galilee.
b: Isaiah 9:2 promises that for those in "the land of deep shadow, / a light shines on them" (Isaiah 9:2, where the Hebrew tsalmavet may be read "shadow of death"), the prophecy that leads into the birth of the child on David's throne (Isaiah 9:6–7). Matthew quotes it when Jesus begins his work in Galilee (Matthew 4:16). Psalm 107:10 speaks of prisoners "sitting in the dark and deep shadow." Luke's Gentile readers would hear in "light" the inclusion of the nations that Simeon will sing about (2:32). "The road of peace" answers Isaiah's lament: "They do not know the way of peace" (Isaiah 59:8).

t: John in the wilderness: the Qumran question
p: Was John raised among the Essenes at Qumran? Possible, but there is no direct evidence.
b: The Judean wilderness by the Dead Sea was home to the community that left the Dead Sea Scrolls, usually identified with the Essenes, who, Josephus says, took in other people's children to raise in their ways (Jewish War 2.120). Both John and the Qumran community used Isaiah 40:3 of themselves, practiced washings, called for repentance and expected God's coming judgment. Some scholars therefore think John grew up at or near Qumran, perhaps after his elderly parents died. Others point to the differences: John's single baptism, his outward preaching to all Israel, and his diet of locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4) rather than a common table. Most say the link is possible but unproven.

a: he kept growing and getting stronger in spirit
p: Luke closes John's childhood as 1 Samuel closes Samuel's. He will do the same for Jesus (2:40, 52).
b: "And the boy Samuel grew up beside the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:21), and "the boy Samuel kept growing up and doing well" (1 Samuel 2:26); Judges 13:24 says the same of Samson. Luke uses nearly identical summaries for John here and for Jesus at 2:40 and 2:52, keeping the two stories in step. "Presented to Israel" (anadeixis, "showing, public appointment") points to John's public appearance in 3:2.

p: Rome's first emperor, hailed as savior and bringer of peace. Luke sets Jesus' birth under his order.
b: Gaius Octavius, Julius Caesar's adopted heir, defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC and ruled the Roman world until AD 14. In 27 BC the Senate gave him the title Augustus, "revered." His reign was celebrated as an age of peace (the Altar of Augustan Peace was dedicated in Rome in 9 BC), and cities of the East honored him as a god and savior; the Priene inscription of 9 BC calls his birthday the beginning of "good news" for the world. Luke's readers would hear the contrast: the emperor gives an order, and the whole world moves, but God uses it to bring the true Savior and the true peace to birth in David's town (2:11, 14).

a: the whole inhabited world was to be registered
p: Oikoumenē meant the Roman Empire. No single empire-wide census under Augustus is known.
b: Oikoumenē, "the inhabited world," was the usual Greek way to speak of the Roman Empire (Acts 11:28; 17:6). Augustus did order many censuses: of Roman citizens (three, which he lists in his own record, the Res Gestae 8), and of provinces such as Gaul and, later, Egypt, where a census every fourteen years is documented. No ancient source except Luke mentions one decree covering the whole empire at once. Some scholars read Luke as summing up Augustus' census policy as a whole; others think Luke has generalized a local census. "Registered" (apographesthai) means being entered on a list for taxation. See the next note on Quirinius.
orig: ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην (apographesthai pasan tēn oikoumenēn)

a: It was the first such registration, carried out while Quirinius governed Syria
p: Josephus dates Quirinius' census of Judea to AD 6, ten years after Herod died. How do the dates fit?
b: Quirinius became governor of Syria in AD 6, when Augustus removed Herod's son Archelaus and put Judea under direct Roman rule; Josephus says Quirinius then took a census of Judea that sparked the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Antiquities 18.1–4, 26), a census Luke knows (Acts 5:37). But Luke 1:5 and Matthew 2:1 put Jesus' birth under Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. Views: (1) Luke joined the birth to the famous later census by mistake (most critical scholars, such as Emil Schürer, Raymond Brown and Joseph Fitzmyer); (2) Quirinius held an earlier post in Syria (William Ramsay); (3) prōtē means "before": "this registration took place before Quirinius governed Syria," possible Greek but strained; (4) an earlier registration or oath under Herod was later remembered by the better-known governor's name. The chapter page sets out the evidence. On all views Matthew and Luke agree that Jesus was born while Herod was king.
orig: αὕτη ἀπογραφὴ πρώτη ἐγένετο ἡγεμονεύοντος τῆς Συρίας Κυρηνίου

a: each one going to his own town
p: Roman censuses usually counted people where they lived or held property, not in ancestral towns.
b: In Roman practice people were registered where they lived and owned land, since the point was taxation. A Greek papyrus from Egypt preserves an order of the prefect Gaius Vibius Maximus (AD 104) telling those living away from their home districts to return there for the census, which shows that "going home" for a registration was known. If Joseph had property or family land in Bethlehem, his journey fits that pattern. Luke's stress, though, is on David's line: Joseph goes to "David's town" because he belongs to David's house (2:4).

p: About 90 miles, several days on foot, and "up" because Jerusalem's hills are higher than Galilee.
b: The road from Nazareth to Bethlehem ran either down the Jordan valley and up through Jericho or south through the hills of Samaria, about 90 miles (145 km). On foot, with a pregnant woman, it would take four days or more. Bethlehem lies about six miles south of Jerusalem in the Judean hills, so the Bible always speaks of going "up" to Judea.

a: David's town, which is called Bethlehem
p: In the Old Testament "the city of David" is Jerusalem. Luke uses the phrase for Bethlehem, David's birthplace.
b: In the Old Testament "the city of David" is the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem that David captured (2 Samuel 5:7, 9). Luke applies the phrase instead to Bethlehem, where David was born and anointed (1 Samuel 16:1–13; 17:12). Micah 5:2 promised a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, which Matthew quotes (Matthew 2:6); Luke does not quote it but makes the same point through the town's name. Bethlehem means "house of bread."
orig: πόλιν Δαυὶδ ἥτις καλεῖται Βηθλέεμ (polin Dauid hētis kaleitai Bēthleem)
r: 2 Samuel 5:7; 2 Samuel 5:9; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; 1 Samuel 17:12; Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6; John 7:42

p: Luke does not say she was required to. She may have been, or Joseph would not leave her behind.
b: Roman law did not always require women to appear in person, though a later jurist, Ulpian, notes that in the province of Syria women were liable to the poll tax from age twelve. Joseph may have been unwilling to leave his pregnant wife, whose condition could cause gossip in Nazareth (compare Matthew 1:19). Luke still calls Mary only "promised in marriage," though they were traveling together and, in Matthew's account, Joseph had taken her into his home (Matthew 1:24–25): the marriage had not been consummated.

p: A legal and religious status: the son who opened the womb. It does not by itself mean later children.
b: Prōtotokos prepares for 2:22–23: a firstborn son belonged to God and had to be presented and redeemed (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). The word does not by itself say that other children followed. A Jewish gravestone from Egypt (Tell el-Yehudiyeh, dated 5 BC) mourns a young mother, Arsinoe, who died giving birth to her "firstborn" child, the only one she ever had. Whether Mary later had other children is a question the churches answer differently; see the card at Matthew 1:25 and the topic Brothers of Jesus.

a: She bound him snugly in strips of cloth
p: Wrapping a newborn tightly in cloth strips was ordinary care. A king was swaddled like everyone else.
b: Babies were washed, rubbed with salt and wrapped tightly in strips of cloth, a sign of a cared-for child; Ezekiel 16:4 describes an abandoned baby who was not. In the Wisdom of Solomon, King Solomon says, "I was nursed in swaddling cloths, with care," because "no king has had any other beginning" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:4–5, paraphrased). The swaddling is not a sign of poverty; the manger is the strange part (2:12).

a: laid him down in a manger
p: A feeding trough for animals. Isaiah 1:3 gave Christian art its ox and donkey.
b: Phatnē is a feeding trough, or the stall where animals ate. In village houses of the region, animals were often brought into a lower part of the family room at night, with feeding troughs cut into the floor or the step, so a manger need not mean a stable apart from the house (Kenneth Bailey). The Greek of Isaiah 1:3 uses the same word: "a donkey knows its master's feeding trough. / Israel does not know" (Isaiah 1:3). From this verse came the ox and donkey of Christmas art (they are first named at the manger in the later Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew). Very early tradition placed the birth in a cave used for animals near Bethlehem (Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 78; Origen, Against Celsus 1.51), over which Constantine built the Church of the Nativity in the 330s.

a: no space for them in the guest room
t: Not an inn: the guest room
p: Kataluma means a lodging or guest room, as in 22:11. There is no innkeeper in Luke.
b: The traditional "no room in the inn" (KJV) has shaped centuries of Christmas plays with a hard-hearted innkeeper, but the text has no innkeeper and probably no inn. Luke's word for a commercial inn is pandocheion (10:34). Kataluma means a place to stay; in 22:11 it is the "guest room" where Jesus eats the Passover. Kenneth Bailey argued that Joseph and Mary stayed with relatives in an ordinary village house whose small guest room was already full, so the baby was laid in a manger in the family's main room. Stephen Carlson argues similarly that the kataluma was the lodging space where they were staying and that it was too small for a birth. Either way the point is not rejection but humble, crowded circumstances. The phrase "there was no space for them" may still carry a hint of the world's lack of welcome that John 1:11 makes explicit.

p: Shepherds recall David and God the shepherd. Were they also despised outsiders? That is debated.
b: Bethlehem's most famous shepherd was David (1 Samuel 16:11), and God is Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34). Many preachers say shepherds were despised outcasts, citing later rabbinic texts that list herding among suspect trades and refuse shepherds as witnesses (for example Mishnah Qiddushin 4:14). Raymond Brown and others caution that those texts are later and that the Bible presents shepherds positively; Luke's shepherds are simple, working people, the lowly whom God lifts (1:52), without needing to be outlaws. They are the first to hear the good news and the first to tell it (2:17).

a: taking turns guarding their flock through the night
p: Luke gives no date or season. December 25 is first certainly attested in a Roman list of AD 354.
b: The phrase phylassontes phylakas means "keeping the watches," night watches in shifts. Some argue that flocks would not be out at night in a Judean winter, so the birth was in spring or autumn; others note that flocks near Bethlehem could be kept out much of the year. Luke does not say. The first certain evidence for December 25 is a Roman calendar of AD 354 (the Chronograph of 354); a passage of Hippolytus (Commentary on Daniel 4.23, about 204) that gives December 25 may be earlier, if it is original, which some scholars doubt. The Eastern churches long kept January 6. Two explanations are given: the church chose the date to replace the Roman winter festival of the Unconquered Sun, or it calculated it by counting nine months from March 25, the traditional date of both the Annunciation and the crucifixion. Scholars still debate which came first.
orig: φυλάσσοντες φυλακὰς τῆς νυκτός (phylassontes phylakas tēs nyktos)

a: the Lord's glory blazed all around them
t: The Lord's glory on a hillside
p: The shining presence that once filled the tabernacle and the temple now appears in a field.
b: "The glory of the Lord" (Hebrew kavod, Greek doxa) is God's visible, shining presence that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35) and Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). Isaiah promised it would appear again: "the glory of the LORD has dawned over you" (Isaiah 60:1), and "the LORD's glory will be revealed, / and all flesh will see it" (Isaiah 40:5). It now shines on shepherds out in the fields, not in the sanctuary where Zechariah served. Later the disciples see Jesus' glory on the mountain (9:32).

a: a great joy that will belong to the whole people
p: Laos, "the people," means Israel. Simeon will widen it to the nations (2:31–32).
b: Luke uses laos for the people of Israel (1:68, 77; 2:32). The good news is first for Israel, as the angel told Zechariah and Mary. Simeon will speak of "all the peoples" (plural) and "the nations" (2:31–32), and Acts carries the message to them. "Joy" is one of Luke's signature words, from the angel's promise to Zechariah (1:14) to the disciples' "great joy" at the end (24:52).
orig: χαρὰν μεγάλην ἥτις ἔσται παντὶ τῷ λαῷ (charan megalēn hētis estai panti tō laō)

p: Luke's "today" marks the moment God's salvation arrives: at the birth, in Nazareth, at Zacchaeus' house, on the cross.
b: Sēmeron is a small word with weight in Luke: Scripture is fulfilled "today" in Nazareth (4:21), salvation comes "today" to Zacchaeus' house (19:9), and the dying criminal will be with Jesus in Paradise "today" (23:43). The promises are not only for a distant future; they arrive in a particular day.

t: A Savior, in the empire of a "savior"
p: Greek cities hailed Augustus as savior. Luke's angel gives the title to a newborn in a manger.
b: Sōtēr was a title of gods and rulers in the Greek world; inscriptions call Augustus "savior" of the world. In the Greek Old Testament God is Israel's savior (Isaiah 45:21), and the judges God raised up were called "saviors" (Judges 3:9, 15). Luke is the only one of the first three Gospels to call Jesus "Savior" (here and Acts 5:31; 13:23); Mary has already called God her Savior (1:47). The announcement to shepherds, in the language of imperial proclamations ("good news," "savior," "peace"), sets Jesus quietly against Caesar.

p: An unusual pair of titles without "the." Some think Luke meant "the Lord's Messiah," as in 2:26.
b: Christos is the Greek for Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one." This site renders it "Messiah" where it is a title and "Christ" where it has become part of Jesus' name; this is its first use in Luke. The phrase christos kyrios, both words without the article, is rare. The same two words appear in the Greek of Lamentations 4:20 and in Psalms of Solomon 17:32, where most scholars think they translate "the LORD's anointed," so some suggest Luke meant "the Lord's Messiah," as Simeon's revelation says in 2:26. Most take the words as two titles side by side, as Peter proclaims in Acts: "God has made him both Lord and Messiah" (Acts 2:36). The KJV's "Christ the Lord" is the traditional English.

p: Isaiah gave a king a sign about a child. Here shepherds get a sign: a baby in a feeding trough.
b: When King Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, Isaiah said, "the Lord will give you a sign himself" (Isaiah 7:14), the birth of a child. The shepherds' sign is not a wonder in the sky but a newborn lying where animals eat. It is a sign in two ways: it identifies the right baby in Bethlehem, and it shows what kind of Lord he is. Later Simeon calls the child "a sign people speak against" (2:34).

p: Stratia is an army. The "host of heaven" sings, not of war, but of peace.
b: Stratia ouranios, "heavenly army," recalls "the LORD of Armies" and the heavenly host around God's throne (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 103:21). The Romans kept the peace of Augustus with legions; this army sings of peace. Luke's crowd of angels praising God anticipates the crowd of disciples praising God at the entry to Jerusalem (19:37–38).

a: Glory to God in the heights above
p: The angels' song became the Gloria of Christian worship. It has a mirror in 19:38.
b: The two lines balance heaven and earth: glory to God in the highest places, peace among people on earth. The Latin Gloria in excelsis Deo grew into the hymn sung in the Mass and in the Orthodox Great Doxology. When Jesus enters Jerusalem, the disciples sing a matching line about peace in heaven and glory in the highest places (19:38): at his birth heaven sings peace to earth; at his entry, as Jerusalem is about to reject him, earth sings peace in heaven.

p: Eudokia here is God's favor, not human "good will." Peace is God's gift to the people he chooses to favor.
b: Eudokia means "good pleasure, favor." With the oldest manuscripts, the phrase anthrōpois eudokias means "people of [his] good pleasure," that is, people on whom God's favor rests. It does not mean "people of good will" (the Latin hominibus bonae voluntatis was often understood that way). Joseph Fitzmyer showed that the Dead Sea Scrolls use the same Hebrew expression, "the sons of his good pleasure," for God's chosen people. The verb comes back at Jesus' baptism, "in you I take delight" (3:22, as in Mark 1:11). The KJV reading is explained in the variant.

a: this word that has come true
p: Rhēma means both "word" and "event," like Hebrew davar. The shepherds go to see a word.
b: The shepherds say, literally, "let us see this rhēma that has happened." Rhēma translates Hebrew davar, which means both "word" and "thing, event." The angel's word has become a thing that can be seen. The same word was Gabriel's ("no word from God will be powerless," 1:37) and Mary's ("as you have said," 1:38); Mary "held on to every one of these words" (2:19).
