orig: τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο τὸ γεγονός (to rhēma touto to gegonos)

a: turning them over in her heart
p: Symballousa means putting things together to find their meaning. Was Mary Luke's source?
b: Symballō is "to throw together, compare, interpret," used of puzzling out the meaning of signs or dreams. The same picture appears when Jacob "kept the matter in mind" after Joseph's dreams (Genesis 37:11) and Daniel kept the vision in his heart (Daniel 7:28). Luke repeats it at 2:51. Many traditional readers have taken these notes as a hint that Mary herself was Luke's source for the birth stories. Critical scholars usually see them as a literary device: Mary as the first believer who keeps God's word and grows in understanding (8:15, 21; 11:28).

a: it was time to circumcise him
p: Jesus enters the covenant of Abraham on the eighth day, like every Jewish boy.
b: Luke records Jesus' circumcision in one verse, but it matters: Jesus is a Jew who keeps the law from his first week. Paul says God sent his Son "born under the law" (Galatians 4:4). The church once kept January 1, the eighth day after Christmas, as the Feast of the Circumcision; Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine note how often Christian art and preaching forgot that Jesus was circumcised. The naming fulfills the angel's command (1:31) and matches John's naming (1:59–63).

p: Luke mentions the law five times in 2:22–39: Jesus' family does everything it requires.
b: In 2:22–39 Luke refers to the law of Moses or "of the Lord" five times (2:22, 23, 24, 27, 39). Two rules are combined: the mother's purification forty days after the birth of a son (Leviticus 12:2–8) and the giving of the firstborn son to God (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). Luke wants Gentile readers to know that Jesus came from a family faithful to Israel's law, and that the temple was his first public setting. Some details are compressed: the firstborn's redemption price of five shekels (Numbers 18:15–16) is not mentioned, and no rule required bringing the baby to the temple.

a: to present him to the Lord
p: The law did not require bringing the baby to the temple. Hannah did bring Samuel.
b: A firstborn son was to be bought back from God for five shekels (Numbers 18:15–16), which could be paid to any priest. Luke does not mention the payment; instead the parents "present" Jesus in the temple, as Hannah brought Samuel to the house of the LORD at Shiloh and gave him to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:22–28). Old Eli at Shiloh and Simeon in Jerusalem, who expects to die soon (2:29), both bless the parents (1 Samuel 2:20; 2:34). Paul uses the same verb when he urges believers to "present" their bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

a: Every male that opens a womb
p: A loose quotation of Exodus 13:2 and 13:12: every firstborn male is holy to the Lord.
b: Exodus 13:2 commands, "Set apart for me as holy every firstborn, the first to open any womb among the Israelites" (Exodus 13:2), and Exodus 13:12–15 explains that firstborn sons are bought back because God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt. Luke's wording is a summary, not an exact quotation of the Greek Old Testament. "Will be called holy" echoes 1:35, "will be called holy, God's Son."

a: a pair of turtledoves or two young doves
p: Leviticus allows two birds instead of a lamb for a mother who cannot afford a sheep.
b: The law asked a new mother to bring a year-old lamb and a bird; but "If she cannot afford a sheep, she is to take two turtledoves or two young doves" (Leviticus 12:8). Mary brings the poor family's offering. Luke, the Gospel most concerned with the poor (1:53; 4:18; 6:20), shows Jesus born into a poor household. Whether Mary needed purifying from sin is a separate question, which the churches answer differently; see the card at Leviticus 12.

p: Luke says only that he was righteous and devout. Tradition made him an old priest.
b: Simeon (Shim'on, "he has heard") is not called a priest or old, though his words in 2:29 suggest he was near death, and tradition pictures him as an aged priest; the Protevangelium of James makes him the successor of Zechariah. Some have identified him with Rabbi Simeon, son of Hillel, but there is no evidence for this. "Careful to honor God" renders eulabēs, "devout," used in Acts of devout Jews (Acts 2:5; 8:2).

p: Isaiah's "Comfort, comfort my people" became a name for the hope of national restoration.
b: Paraklēsis, "comfort, consolation," points to Isaiah 40–66, which begins, "Comfort, comfort my people" (Isaiah 40:1), and promises the end of exile, God's return to Zion and his servant's light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6, 13). Simeon belongs to those in Israel who were "looking forward" to it, like Anna's circle "looking for Jerusalem to be redeemed" (2:38) and Joseph of Arimathea later (23:51). Later rabbinic tradition even gave the Messiah the name Menachem, "Comforter."

p: The Old Testament phrase "the LORD's anointed" for Israel's king.
b: Ton christon kyriou is the Greek Old Testament's phrase for the anointed king: David would not harm Saul, "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:6), and the kings of the earth rise "against the LORD and against his anointed one" (Psalm 2:2). The Psalms of Solomon, written by Jews in the first century BC, hope for a Davidic king they call "the Lord's anointed" (Psalms of Solomon 18:5, 7). Simeon is promised he will not die before seeing him.
r: 1 Samuel 24:6; Psalm 2:2; Psalms of Solomon 18:5–7; 9:20; Acts 4:26

a: Simeon received him into his arms
p: The Orthodox call this feast the Meeting; in the West it is the Presentation, or Candlemas.
b: The churches keep this scene on February 2, forty days after Christmas. The Orthodox name it the Hypapante, "Meeting," because the old man Simeon, representing Israel, meets the Lord in his temple. In the West it is the Presentation of the Lord, also called Candlemas, because candles are blessed for the "light to bring revelation to the nations" (2:32). Icons show Simeon holding the child with covered hands, as one holds something holy.

a: now you are setting your slave free
p: Apolyeis is the verb for releasing a slave, or letting someone go. Simeon may be asking to die in peace.
b: Simeon calls God despota, "Master," and himself doulos, "slave." Apolyeis means "you release" or "you dismiss": the word for setting a slave free or discharging a sentry from duty, and a gentle way of speaking of death (compare Genesis 15:15, going to one's fathers "in peace"). The Latin opening, Nunc dimittis, gives the song its name. The church sings it at night prayer (Compline), and the Anglican Prayer Book at Evening Prayer, as a prayer to go to rest in peace, and it is sung at many Christian funerals.
orig: νῦν ἀπολύεις τὸν δοῦλόν σου, δέσποτα (nyn apolyeis ton doulon sou, despota)

p: Isaiah promised that every far end of the earth would see how God saves. Acts ends on the same note.
b: "Every far end of the earth / will see how our God saves" (Isaiah 52:10), and in the Greek of Isaiah 40:5, "all flesh will see the salvation of God," which Luke quotes at 3:6. Simeon has seen it in a baby. Luke-Acts ends with Paul in Rome saying, "this salvation from God has been sent out to the Gentiles" (Acts 28:28): Simeon's words frame the whole two-volume work.

a: a light to bring revelation to the nations
t: A light for the nations, glory for Israel
p: Isaiah's servant is a light to the nations. Simeon keeps Israel's glory beside it.
b: God said to his servant, "I will give you as a light to the nations" (Isaiah 49:6; compare Isaiah 42:6), and Paul and Barnabas quote this when they turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:47; compare Acts 26:23). Simeon's two lines are balanced: revelation for the nations, glory for God's people Israel (Isaiah 46:13). The child does not take Israel's glory away to give to others; he is Israel's glory. Whether that balance holds in the rest of Luke-Acts is one of the great debates about Luke (Jacob Jervell argues it does; Jack Sanders that Luke ends with Israel rejected).
r: Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 42:6; Isaiah 46:13; Acts 13:47; Acts 26:23; Acts 28:28

p: After all they have been told, Joseph and Mary are still amazed. Understanding comes slowly.
b: Readers sometimes ask why Mary and Joseph wonder at Simeon's words after the angels' messages. Luke often notes amazement as people's first response to God's acts (1:63; 2:18); it is not disbelief. The parents learn gradually, and at 2:50 they will not understand at all.

a: for many in Israel to fall and to rise
p: Isaiah's stone that some trip over. Is it the same people who fall and rise, or two groups?
b: Keitai, "is set," can describe a stone laid in place. Isaiah spoke of God as "a rock they trip over, / for both houses of Israel" (Isaiah 8:14), and of a cornerstone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16); Jesus will apply the stone image to himself (20:17–18). Readers take "fall and rise" as (1) two groups: some in Israel will stumble over him and some will be raised up, as the reversals of Luke suggest; or (2) the same people: many will fall (in repentance, or in judgment) and then rise again, a reading some find in the hope of Israel's restoration. The Greek anastasis, "rising," is also the word for resurrection.
orig: κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν (keitai eis ptōsin kai anastasin pollōn)

p: The same verb ends Acts: the Christian movement "is spoken against everywhere."
b: Antilegomenon, "spoken against, opposed." At the end of Luke's second volume the Jewish leaders in Rome tell Paul about the Christian movement, "we know it is spoken against everywhere" (Acts 28:22). Simeon's prophecy reaches from the child to the church: Jesus and his followers will be a sign that divides.

a: a sword will run right through your soul
p: Grief at the cross, a sword of division, or doubt? The fathers and modern scholars read it differently.
b: Rhomphaia is a large sword. Readings: (1) Mary's grief at her son's death, as at the cross in John 19:25, which became the Western devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows and the hymn Stabat Mater; (2) a sword of division that will cut through Israel and even through Mary's own family, so that she too must choose (8:19–21; 11:27–28; 12:51–53), the view of Raymond Brown and others; (3) Origen (Homilies on Luke 17) suggested the sword was doubt that would pierce even Mary at the cross, a view later Catholic writers rejected; (4) Epiphanius mentions, without accepting it, a view that Mary would die a violent death, and Ambrose denied that the sword meant a violent death, since neither Scripture nor history says so (Exposition of Luke 2.61). The Greek Old Testament uses the image of a sword going through the land as judgment (Ezekiel 14:17).
orig: σοῦ δὲ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται ῥομφαία

a: Anna, Phanuel's daughter, from Asher's tribe
t: Anna of the tribe of Asher
p: Hannah again, a prophetess, from one of the northern tribes that were thought "lost."
b: Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, the name of Samuel's mother, whose song Mary echoed. She is a prophētis, like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), and Philip's daughters later (Acts 21:9). She is from Asher, one of the northern tribes exiled by Assyria; many families of those tribes in fact kept their identity in Galilee and the dispersion, and Richard Bauckham suggests her family may have come from the Asher community in Media, the setting of Tobit. Phanuel is the Greek form of Penuel, "face of God" (Genesis 32:30). With Simeon she forms a pair, a man and a woman, as Luke often pairs stories.
r: 1 Samuel 1:2; Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14; Acts 21:9; Genesis 32:30

t: Eighty-four years old, or a widow for eighty-four years?
p: The Greek can mean she was eighty-four, or that she had been a widow for 84 years, which would make her about 105, Judith's age.
b: Heōs etōn ogdoēkonta tessarōn, "up to eighty-four years," can mean her age or the length of her widowhood. If the second, married at about fourteen, seven years a wife and eighty-four a widow, she would be about 105, exactly the age at which the widow Judith died (Judith 16:23), and like Judith she lived a life of fasting and prayer (Judith 8:4–6). Most translations take the first reading; Richard Bauckham and others favor the second and see the echo of Judith deliberate. "She did not leave the temple" probably means she was there every day, not that she lived in it. The Byzantine text and the KJV read "about" for "until" (see the variant).
orig: ἕως ἐτῶν ὀγδοήκοντα τεσσάρων (heōs etōn ogdoēkonta tessarōn)

p: Anna's hearers hoped for the promise of Isaiah 52:9: "he has bought Jerusalem back."
b: Isaiah sang, "The LORD has comforted his people; / he has bought Jerusalem back" (Isaiah 52:9). Simeon waited for the "comforting of Israel" (2:25), Anna's circle for the "redemption of Jerusalem." Coins of the Jewish revolts against Rome (AD 66–70 and 132–135) carried slogans of freedom and redemption for Zion and Israel. Luke presents faithful Jews in the temple, men and women, as the first to welcome Jesus.

t: Luke and Matthew on Jesus' infancy
p: Luke goes straight from the temple to Nazareth. Matthew has the magi, the flight to Egypt and a later move to Nazareth.
b: In Luke the family lives in Nazareth, travels to Bethlehem for the census, and returns home after forty days. In Matthew the family seems to live in Bethlehem, the magi visit a "house" (Matthew 2:11), they flee to Egypt from Herod, and only later settle in Nazareth (Matthew 2:22–23). Harmonizers since the church fathers place the magi and Egypt after the presentation, with a return to Bethlehem, or read Luke's "went back to Galilee" as a summary that skips them. Most critical scholars (for example Raymond Brown), holding that Luke did not know Matthew, see two independent traditions agreeing on key points (Herod's reign, Mary and Joseph, a virginal conception, birth in Bethlehem, a home in Nazareth) but not fully reconcilable in their order. On the Farrer view, Luke knew Matthew and retold the story his own way. See the chapter page.

p: The law called men to the three pilgrimage feasts. Women and children went too, as Hannah did.
b: The law commanded every male to appear before the LORD three times a year, at Passover, Weeks and Booths (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16). Many families from Galilee went at least once a year, and women and children often came, as Elkanah's family went up to Shiloh year after year (1 Samuel 1:3, 7, 21). Josephus describes crowds of hundreds of thousands at Passover. The scene foreshadows Jesus' final Passover journey to Jerusalem (9:51; 22:1).

p: The bar mitzvah ceremony is medieval. Twelve was simply the edge of adulthood.
b: It is often said that Jesus went to Jerusalem for his bar mitzvah. The ceremony is much later (it is first described in the Middle Ages). The Mishnah says a boy becomes obliged to keep the commandments at thirteen (Mishnah Avot 5:21), and twelve was the threshold of adult responsibility. Josephus says Samuel began to prophesy at twelve (Antiquities 5.348), and Jewish tradition gave the same age for wise boys such as Solomon and Daniel. Luke shows Jesus on the edge of adulthood, already wise in God's law.

p: Villagers traveled to the feasts together. A boy of twelve could be anywhere in the group.
b: Synodia is a traveling company. Families from the same villages went to the feasts together for safety and company, and a twelve-year-old would be treated as nearly grown, free to walk with relatives and friends. That Joseph and Mary went a full day before missing him fits such travel; it is not a sign of neglect.

p: A practical detail, or a hint of the three days of Jesus' death and resurrection?
b: The count is natural: a day's journey out, a day back and a day of searching, or three days counted from their departure. But many readers notice that the parents lost Jesus at Passover and found him "after three days" in his Father's house, and hear an early hint of his death and rising "on the third day" at a later Passover (9:22; 24:7, 21, 46). Luke's wording here (meta hēmeras treis) is not his usual resurrection phrase, so the link is possible but not certain.

a: sitting in the middle of the teachers
p: Jesus listens and asks questions: the way Jewish learning worked. He is not lecturing them.
b: Teachers of the law gathered students in the temple's colonnades. Jesus sits "in the middle," the place of a learner in a circle, "hearing" and "putting questions," the normal method of Jewish study; the amazement is at his understanding and his answers (2:47). Later legends turned him into a child prodigy who silenced his teachers, as in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, and Christian art often shows Jesus lecturing the doctors. Luke's scene is more modest and more Jewish. It foreshadows Jesus teaching daily in the temple in his last week (19:47; 21:37).

p: Mary speaks of Joseph as "your father." Jesus answers by speaking of his Father, God.
b: Luke has no problem calling Joseph Jesus' "father" and the two "his parents" (2:27, 33, 41, 43): Joseph is his father in law and in daily life. But Mary's "your father" sets up Jesus' first recorded words, which speak of "my Father" (2:49), the first time in Luke that Jesus calls God his Father. "In agony" (odynōmenoi) is a strong word, used later of the rich man's torment in Hades (16:24–25).
orig: ὁ πατήρ σου κἀγὼ ὀδυνώμενοι (ho patēr sou kagō odynōmenoi)

t: "I must": the first words of Jesus
p: Dei, "it is necessary," marks God's plan in Luke. Jesus' first words already use it.
b: Dei, "it must be," is one of Luke's key words for God's purpose: Jesus "must" preach in other towns (4:43), the Son of Man "must suffer" (9:22; 17:25), "must" stay at Zacchaeus' house (19:5), and everything written about him "must be fulfilled" (24:44). The first words Jesus speaks in the Gospel already put his life under that divine necessity.

t: "In my Father's house" or "about my Father's business"?
p: The Greek says "in the things of my Father." Most read "house"; the KJV read "business." Both are possible.
b: En tois tou patros mou is literally "in the [ ] of my Father," with the noun left out. Greek used this idiom for "in someone's house" (the Greek of Esther 7:9 speaks of a gallows "in Haman's," meaning at his house), and the setting, a search ending in the temple, favors "my Father's house," the reading of most modern translations. But the phrase can also mean "about my Father's affairs," as the Latin Vulgate (in his quae Patris mei sunt) and the KJV ("about my Father's business") took it. The Plain says "at my Father's," which keeps something of the Greek's openness: the temple is his Father's house, and his Father's business is where he must be.
orig: ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου (en tois tou patros mou)

p: After this one scene, Luke is silent about Jesus' life until about age thirty (3:23).
b: Hypotassomenos, "being subject," shows the Son of God keeping the commandment to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12). Between 2:52 and 3:23 lie about eighteen years of which the Gospels say nothing except that Jesus was known as a builder's son in Nazareth (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). Later apocryphal gospels, such as the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, filled the gap with miracle stories that the church never accepted. Catholic and Orthodox devotion honors the "hidden life" at Nazareth and the Holy Family as a model for families; Protestant writers, too, have found in these years a dignity for ordinary work.

a: Jesus kept moving forward in wisdom and in maturity
p: Luke says Jesus truly grew, in wisdom and in favor with God. How does that fit belief in his divinity?
b: The sentence echoes 1 Samuel: "the boy Samuel kept growing up and doing well, in the eyes of the LORD and of people too" (1 Samuel 2:26), and Proverbs 3:4. Hēlikia can mean "age" or "stature" (in 19:3 Zacchaeus is small in hēlikia); "maturity" covers both. Early Christians argued over what it means that Jesus "grew in wisdom." Arians used it to argue that the Son was less than the Father; Athanasius answered that Luke speaks of the Son's human nature (Orations against the Arians 3.51–53). The Council of Chalcedon (451) later defined Christ as one person, fully divine and fully human, "like us in all things apart from sin," which left room for a real human growth. Cyril of Alexandria, Thomas Aquinas and later theologians explained this in different ways, and some modern writers ("kenotic" theologians, from Philippians 2:7) say the Son freely limited his knowledge. Luke simply affirms a real human childhood.
orig: προέκοπτεν σοφίᾳ καὶ ἡλικίᾳ καὶ χάριτι (proekopten sophia kai hēlikia kai chariti)
